text.title: AI Over-Reliance Self-Audit Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules governing what the self-audit measures and how. Each rule replaces a self-report item with a measurement the operator cannot flatter, and each is checkable against the filled checklist, the repository, or the tracker.

rule.statement: Every audit period MUST include at least one timed task performed with completion, chat and agent modes disabled — record the task, wall-clock time, whether it finished, and how many API lookups it needed. A period with no unassisted sample scores 0 on this item regardless of the operator's confidence.

rationale.source: Parasuraman & Riley, "Humans and Automation: Use, Misuse, Disuse, Abuse", Human Factors 1997 — automation-induced skill degradation

rule.rationale: Degradation is invisible while the automation works, because the operator's output is unchanged; it appears only when the aid is removed. An audit that never removes the aid measures the tool, not the operator, and reports full health right up to the outage or rate-limit that exposes the gap.

rule.statement: The audit MUST place the operator's estimated speedup next to a measured one pulled from the repository or tracker over the same window — commits or PRs merged, first-commit-to-merge lead time, tasks closed — and record both numbers plus their sign. An item that records only the estimate fails.

rationale.source: METR, "Measuring the Impact of Early-2025 AI on Experienced Open-Source Developer Productivity" (2025): 16 experienced developers, 246 tasks — forecast ~24% faster, believed ~20% faster afterwards, measured 19% slower

rule.rationale: Self-estimated speed and measured speed diverged in sign, not just magnitude, and the developers still believed the estimate after the fact. Any audit item that ends at the estimate therefore records the belief the audit exists to test.

rule.statement: Any throughput item MUST be paired with a stability item measured over the same window: change-failure rate, count of `git revert` commits, rollbacks, or hotfixes shipped within 24h of a release. A throughput-only checklist is rejected.

rationale.source: DORA, Accelerate State of DevOps Report 2024 — a 25% rise in AI adoption tracked with ~1.5% lower delivery throughput and ~7.2% lower delivery stability

rule.rationale: Assistant usage moves throughput and stability in different directions, so a checklist that watches only volume shows a clean pass while the defect escape rate climbs. Stability is the leading indicator here and the one the operator has no felt sense of.

rule.statement: The read-before-accept item MUST be measured on a random sample of at least 10 AI-attributed hunks from the period (sampled via the commit trailer, agent log, or session transcript). For each, the operator states the control flow and error path from memory before reopening the file; the item's score is the share correct, not a remembered impression.

rationale.source: Lee et al., "The Impact of Generative AI on Critical Thinking", CHI 2025 — higher confidence in the assistant associated with reduced critical-thinking effort

rule.rationale: Reading generated code is fluent, and fluency is misread as comprehension, so recall-based self-report is biased upward exactly where reliance is highest. Forcing a recall test against a random sample converts an impression into a score the operator can fail.

rule.statement: The audit MUST carry at least one tool-computed code-health number trended across periods — duplicate-block ratio from jscpd or PMD-CPD, and the share of lines added in the period that were rewritten or reverted within two weeks. Subjective quality items ("code feels clean") do not satisfy this rule.

rationale.source: GitClear code-quality analysis of ~150M changed lines (2024 edition) — duplicated blocks rose sharply while moved lines, the refactoring signal, declined

rule.rationale: The characteristic assistant failure is not a wrong line but a second copy of a right one: the model regenerates rather than extracts, so duplication grows while every individual diff looks correct at review. Only a repository-wide count sees it; per-diff judgement structurally cannot.

rule.statement: Each failed item MUST map to a named drill with a date and a completion check — failed baseline → next utility function written with the assistant off; failed read-rate → next 10 agent hunks reviewed in a diff tool before staging; failed duplication trend → one extraction refactor of the highest-duplication file. "Be more careful" and "pay more attention" are rejected as remediation entries.

rationale.source: Internal — remediation follow-through audits on recurring self-audits

rule.rationale: Intent-shaped remediation has no completion state, so the next period's audit cannot tell whether it happened and quietly copies it forward. A drill with a date either shows up in the log or does not, which is what makes a repeated failure visible as a trend instead of a mood.

rule.statement: Do NOT run when (a) assistant usage in the period was under about an hour a week — the sample is too small for any item to move; (b) the operator works under peer review that already inspects every diff before merge, which covers the read-rate and stability items; (c) no measurement source exists for the period (no repository history, no tracker, no agent log) — the audit would consist entirely of self-report, the one instrument the rule set above exists to replace.
rule.rationale: Every rule here trades a self-report for a measurement; with no measurable substrate the artefact degrades back to the introspection it was designed to distrust, and a filled-in pass then licenses the reliance it was meant to detect.
